title: Why a 98%-accurate model leaves an agent's state right only 21% of the time
content:
AXI: The Cure for the Cost Crisis in AI
Authors/Creators
Description
AXI is a host-side layer that holds the exact state of an AI job outside the chat, checks every reply with a deterministic gate before it is applied, and sends the model a short fresh prompt at every step. This paper reports pre-registered tests on Gemini 3.8 Flash, open models, an NVIDIA T4 and L4 and a Google TPU v6e: exact state on 1,500 of 1,500 steps, prompts 169 times smaller on average, one exact step 4.5 to 9.3 times cheaper, and up to 185 times more sessions per chip (memory headroom). Predictions were hash-locked before each run and every figure can be recomputed from the saved files. The architecture is by Rajnish Choubey; the tests were built and run by Shalendra Gaur. Code and tests: https://github.com/gaurshalendra2412/axi-runtime

report.summary: A 98%-accurate model compounds to roughly 21% correct agent state after ~75 steps — AXI proposes moving exact state outside the model and gating every reply.
report.background: Agent loops fail arithmetically, not just qualitatively: at 98% per-step reliability, 0.98^75 ≈ 0.21, so a long-running agent's state is correct end-to-end only about one time in five. Every retry, tool call and reformatting step multiplies the odds of silent drift, and because the transcript is the de facto state store, one bad turn poisons every later turn. Meanwhile, context windows balloon: agents re-send full history each step, inflating token bills and memory footprint per concurrent session. The dominant fix so far has been bigger models, better prompting or retrieval — all of which raise per-step accuracy without changing the multiplicative structure of the problem. AXI argues the fix is architectural: keep authoritative state in a host-side store, treat the model as a stateless proposal engine, and validate each proposal deterministically before committing. The paper reports pre-registered tests on Gemini 3.8 Flash, open models, NVIDIA T4/L4 and Google TPU v6e.
key_points: Compounding is the real bottleneck: at 98% per step, ~75 steps leaves about 21% chance the state is still exactly right. Because errors are silent — a plausible but wrong field value — agents rarely crash; they drift. Longer horizons, more tools and more retries all push reliability down geometrically while per-step benchmarks look reassuringly high.

AXI inverts the usual design: authoritative state lives in a host-side layer outside the chat, the model receives a short, freshly assembled prompt each step, and every reply passes a deterministic gate before it is applied. The model becomes a suggestion engine; nothing it says mutates state unless the gate accepts it.

Reported results are striking: exact state on 1,500 of 1,500 steps, prompts averaging 169x smaller, a single exact step 4.5–9.3x cheaper, and up to 185x more concurrent sessions per chip thanks to memory headroom. Tests span Gemini 3.8 Flash, open models, NVIDIA T4/L4 and a Google TPU v6e.

The methodology is unusually disciplined for a white paper: predictions were hash-locked before each run, and every reported figure can be recomputed from saved files in the public repo. That is closer to pre-registered science than typical vendor benchmarking, and it makes the claims falsifiable rather than merely promotable.

Caveats remain. This is a self-published Zenodo paper from a two-person team with no independent replication, and the named model 'Gemini 3.8 Flash' does not correspond to any publicly released Gemini version, which invites scrutiny of the exact test configuration before the numbers are treated as general.
report.impact: If the results generalize, the implications are structural rather than incremental. Developers would stop paying for giant contexts to carry state and start paying for small, targeted prompts plus a validation layer — shifting engineering effort from prompt craft to schema design, gates and state stores. Cost per reliable task could fall by an order of magnitude, making long-horizon agents economically viable where they currently are not, and letting far more sessions run per accelerator. For users, the visible change would be agents that fail loudly instead of quietly, and that survive hundred-step workflows. The broader lesson is that reliability is an architecture problem, not a model-weight problem — though independent replication is needed before the specific multipliers are trusted.
report.tools: Start with the AXI runtime itself (github.com/gaurshalendra2412/axi-runtime), which ships code and reproducible tests. Related patterns worth studying: LangGraph's checkpointers and durable execution for host-side state, Temporal for deterministic workflow orchestration, JSON-Schema constrained decoding (Outlines, Guidance, provider structured outputs) as a lightweight gate, and Pydantic or Zod validation as the commit boundary. Combining a state store with schema-gated writes is the cheapest way to test the paper's core claim on your own workload.
